claims.text: The baseline W–Cu composite contains discrete tungsten and copper phases.
The baseline W–Cu composite has abrupt, unengineered metal–metal interfaces.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 1–2 vol% high-purity graphene nanoplatelets during powder mixing.
Spark plasma sintering can be used to consolidate the graphene-modified composite.
Uniformly dispersed graphene nanoplatelets will form an interfacial network between the tungsten and copper phases.
The graphene addition will create a graded, graphene-enhanced interface bridging the W–Cu boundary.
Graphene nanoplatelets possess extremely high in-plane thermal conductivity.
Uniformly distributed graphene nanoplatelets can act as conductive bridges at W–Cu interfaces.
The graphene conductive bridges will reduce thermal boundary resistance at W–Cu interfaces.
Graphene nanoplatelets can impede crack propagation in the W–Cu composite.
Impeding crack propagation will help preserve the composite's mechanical integrity.
The graphene reinforcement will help maintain radiation-damage resistance.
The graphene-enhanced composite will have thermal conductivity several percent higher, potentially approaching a 10% improvement, than the graphene-free control.
The graphene-enhanced composite will retain mechanical strength similar to that of the graphene-free control.
The graphene-enhanced composite will retain irradiation resistance similar to that of the graphene-free control.
The predicted benefits apply under moderate-to-high temperatures, cyclic thermal loading, and irradiation relevant to fusion-reactor joints.
The predicted benefits require low graphene volume fractions and uniform dispersion.
Excess graphene or graphene agglomeration could degrade mechanical properties or processing consistency.
The magnitude of thermal-conductivity enhancement and the mechanical and irradiation responses depend critically on processing parameters and dispersion quality.
A thermal-conductivity improvement below 5%, or degradation of mechanical durability or irradiation resistance relative to the control, will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction allows an increase described broadly as 'several percent,' which could include values below 5%, while the falsification rule declares any improvement below 5% falsifying. The rule also conflates statistical significance with a fixed effect-size threshold.
